notes: Continuity audit 2026-10-18 applied: s119 Mali's diary opens 'Neithiwr. Daeth negesydd …' (she writes it the night after the feast; echoes the Ddoe / Neithiwr / Heddiw pattern of 12).

Codex review 2026-10-18 applied: C5 model 'yn elyn'; s092 'Ofynnodd y negesydd am fwyd?'; C1 'yn ei gasglu'; A3/A4/A6 accept colloquial fod e / bod hi; A7 accepts a / os ydy (no compulsory backshift; explanation added); nodyn_en distinguishes full and colloquial pronoun forms; s018 'Fydda i byth yn eillio …'; s033 'ond roedd un ochr yn fyr iawn'. Verdicts recorded on all review questions.

Target G33 is narrowed to one core: bod-reporting after a past verb. Reported statements (dwedodd X fod …, ei fod e …, ei bod hi …) and reported yes/no questions (gofynnodd X a / os oedd …) occur about 30 times, mostly in three retelling scenes: the morning council, Mali's retelling to Modlen (who missed the messenger) and Mali's diary. Each reported sentence has its direct-speech original earlier in the chapter, so the contrast meddai ↔ dwedodd … fod is built from the chapter itself.

y byddai appears once (Mali to Modlen), glossed '= "bydd …" (ddoe)' and immediately followed by the direct quotation of the threat ('Ei eiriau fe oedd: Bydd Rhita'n dod!'); it is listed as an incidental and is never tested.
Dafi's one deliberate error ('dwedodd e bod rhyfel yn dod') contrasts with the chapter target (dwedodd + fod) and is corrected by Mali at once.

Open-slot words (CorCenCC top 2000): erbyn (302) and neu (37) for the plan's demand 'Anfon dy farf erbyn y lleuad newydd, neu bydd Rhita'n dod!'; darn (442) for the lock of Cynyr's beard (the 'deposit' is shown as 'Dyma'r dechrau … darn o farf Cynyr nawr, a barf y brenin wedyn' rather than with a word for deposit); achos (576) because Mali's and Arthur's reasons need it. neb is already known from Pennod 26's open slots.
Form added: dwedodd (cy-dweud) and gofynnodd (cy-gofyn), preterite 3sg, already licensed at 33 by the plan's new_forms.

Continuity: Rhita's cloak shows the beards of the kings of Iwerddon (red) and Llydaw (black), matching Pennod 37 as written. The messenger cuts a long gold lock from one side of Cynyr's beard and takes it away with the cloak (Mali recovers it in 37). The deadline is the new moon, two weeks away (Mali). Modlen missed the messenger (she was in the kitchen) and decides on a wool beard; nothing in this chapter decides the plan or the journey (34).

Checker warnings justified: 'a oedd' lint-a-ac hits are the interrogative particle a in reported questions (gofynnodd e a oedd …), not the conjunction; three local-density warnings fall in Mali's retelling and the council, where this chapter's own words (bygwth, bygythiad, rhyfel, heddwch, rhybuddio) recur after being introduced and glossed earlier in the chapter; the near-duplicate pair is Mali's correction of Dafi's deliberate error and his corrected repeat.

Length about 1,530 words against 1,690 (window from 1,521): the chapter ends on Mali's diary and Modlen sewing; no padding added. Mean sentence length is kept in the Rhan 4 window by splitting only very long multi-sentence turns.

Recall pass 2026-10-18: recurrences for Penodau 28–32 vocabulary (swyddogol, gwisg, nerfus, urddas, gwaedd, gwthio, bai, poeni, dathlu, gwin, cerddoriaeth, amddiffyn, grym, cyfrifol, cadw, yn hytrach, dadl, esgob, coginio, dawnsio, seremoni, ai, gwahodd, croesawu, taw, derbyn, mewn gwirionedd, coroni, gwnïo); Modlen's question chain to Mali (Gafodd e ei wahodd? … Naddo, a naddo) echoes Pennod 32. cover.alt: In the great hall at Caerllion the huge messenger holds up the long cloak of beards before the throne; the hall laughs at the beardless boy-king.
cover.art_brief: The great hall of the castle at Caerllion at night (Caerllion palette: red brick and timber, torches, a big hearth, a red-dragon banner on green and white). Rhita's messenger (a huge man, taller than the doorway, long grey snow-dusted hooded cloak, big boots, broad pale face) stands in the middle of the hall holding up the cloak of beards (long tufts of beard hair in red, gold, black, grey and white stitched together in rows; no faces; comic, never gory) so that it hangs down to his boots, pointing with one big finger at a red beard and a long black beard on it. On the tall throne Arthur (12, untidy brown hair with a cowlick, freckles; plain blue cloak over a long blue robe with a small red dragon on the chest) wearing the too-big gold crown sits very straight with a smooth, beardless face. The whole hall laughs: Cai (15, tall, red-blond, rust-red tunic, red cloak, sword at his belt) beside the throne laughs loudest; lords, knights and maids round the tables laugh; Cynyr (broad, huge golden-blond beard to mid-chest, brown cloak with round silver brooch) laughs into his huge golden beard; Mali (12, long dark braid, dark-blue dress, satchel) giggles behind her hand by the throne; only Arthur sits calm and straight. Myrddin (very old, thin, long white beard, round wire spectacles, patched deep-blue robe, tall black brimmed hat) watches from the hearth, a wisp of smoke from his hat. No text.

segments.text: Safodd y negesydd enfawr ar ei draed, ac roedd ei ben e'n agos at y to.

segments.text: "Mae Rhita wedi gorchfygu llawer o frenhinoedd, ac mae e wedi cymryd eu barfau nhw.

inference_aids.alt: The messenger cuts a long lock from one side of Cynyr's huge golden beard with a knife while Cynyr stares in horror, Elen reaches out to him, Arthur stands with one hand raised and the red-bearded lord clutches his own beard.
inference_aids.art_brief: Close scene in the same hall at Caerllion (torchlight, red brick, timber). Rhita's messenger (a huge man, taller than the doorway, long grey snow-dusted hooded cloak, big boots, broad pale face) leans over Cynyr (broad, huge golden-blond beard to mid-chest, brown cloak with round silver brooch) and with a short knife cuts a long golden lock from one side of his huge beard, grinning; the lock hangs from his big fist. Cynyr's mouth is open in horror; one side of his beard is now short. Behind them the big red-bearded lord (Barf Goch) clutches his own beard; Arthur (12, untidy brown hair with a cowlick, freckles; plain blue cloak over a long blue robe with a small red dragon on the chest) (crown) has risen from the throne and stands on the floor with one hand raised; Elen (about fifty, white linen veil, forest-green dress, ring of keys) reaches towards Cynyr. The cloak of beards is slung over the messenger's shoulder. No text.

inference_aids.art_brief: The big castle kitchen at Caerllion in the morning (warm firelight, a big bread oven, copper pots, stacked clean dishes). Modlen (short, round, rosy, white headscarf, long floury apron, big wooden spoon) has opened a big basket of white and black wool (the wool from the fair) and holds a thick bundle of black wool under her nose and chin like a huge black beard, eyebrows raised, wooden spoon in her other hand. Mali (12, long dark braid, dark-blue dress, satchel) laughs with her wax tablet under her arm; Dafi (cup-sized red dragon, two short cream horns, tiny bat wings, big yellow eyes; small enough to sit in a wooden drinking cup) sits on top of the warm oven laughing, a puff of grey smoke from his nose. No text.

grammar.nodyn_en:
This chapter is about reported speech: telling someone what another person said or asked, instead of quoting their exact words. Mali does this for a whole scene, because Modlen was in the kitchen when the messenger came.

In Pennod 22 you met bod clauses after a verb in the present: Mae'r beirdd yn dweud bod Rhita'n byw ar ben yr Wyddfa ('The bards say that Rhita lives on top of Snowdon'). A bod clause replaces mae (or dw i, rwyt ti and so on), and it already means 'that … is', so Welsh needs no separate word for 'that'. After a past verb such as dwedodd ('said') or rhybuddiodd ('warned'), the same bod takes the soft mutation and becomes fod. Compare Mali's two reports about Cynyr: Mae e'n dweud bod ei farf e'n oer ar un ochr ('He says that his beard is cold on one side'), but Dwedodd Cynyr fod ei farf e'n oer ar un ochr ('Cynyr said that his beard was cold on one side').

Here are quoted words and their reports side by side:
- "Mae Rhita'n casglu barfau," meddai'r negesydd ('"Rhita is collecting beards," said the messenger') → Dwedodd y negesydd fod Rhita'n casglu barfau ('The messenger said that Rhita was collecting beards').
- "Rhaid i ni gasglu byddin!" meddai Barf Goch ('"We must gather an army!" said Barf Goch') → Dwedodd Barf Goch fod rhaid casglu byddin fawr ('Barf Goch said that a big army had to be gathered').
- Dwedodd e fod clogyn o farfau gyda'r cawr ('He said that the giant had a cloak of beards').

Notice that Welsh does not turn mae into roedd. English moves a reported verb into the past ('is' becomes 'was', 'is collecting' becomes 'was collecting'), but Welsh uses the same fod. The construction after fod stays as it was in the quotation (yn + verb-noun, wedi + verb-noun, rhaid, gyda); only pronouns change with the speaker's point of view. With wedi, English uses 'had': Dwedodd e fod Rhita wedi gorchfygu llawer o frenhinoedd ('He said that Rhita had defeated many kings'). With rhaid: Dwedodd e fod rhaid i Arthur anfon ei farf erbyn y lleuad newydd ('He said that Arthur had to send his beard by the new moon').

When the subject of the reported sentence is a pronoun, the clause starts with a possessive and bod, as in Pennod 22 (fy mod i, dy fod di, ei fod e, ei bod hi, ein bod ni, eu bod nhw). The person changes just as it does in English: Cai said "Dw i eisiau ymladd" ('I want to fight'), and Mali reports it as Dwedodd Cai ei fod e eisiau ymladd yn erbyn y cawr ('Cai said that he wanted to fight against the giant'). For a woman: Dwedodd hi ei bod hi'n brysur ('She said that she was busy'). These forms do not change after a past verb; only the bare bod becomes fod. To add a second clause, a ('and') and ei join as a'i: Dwedodd e fod Rhita wedi gorchfygu llawer o frenhinoedd, a'i fod e wedi casglu eu barfau nhw ('He said that Rhita had defeated many kings, and that he had collected their beards'). For a negative, ddim follows the subject of the clause: Dwedodd Arthur ei fod e eisiau heddwch, ond ei fod e ddim yn ofni'r cawr ('Arthur said that he wanted peace, but that he wasn't afraid of the giant').

Rhybuddio ('to warn') works the same way, with the person warned straight after the verb. That person is the object of an inflected verb, so it takes the soft mutation (pawb → bawb): Rhybuddiodd Myrddin bawb fod Rhita'n gawr balch ac yn elyn peryglus ('Myrddin warned everyone that Rhita was a proud giant and a dangerous enemy').

Dafi makes this chapter's deliberate mistake: A dwedodd e bod rhyfel yn dod! Mali corrects him: Fod, Dafi. Dwedodd e fod rhyfel yn dod ('He said that war was coming'). After a reporting verb in the past, this book always gives bare bod as fod. With a pronoun subject, keep the personal form: ei fod e, ei bod hi, and so on.

Reported yes/no questions use gofynnodd ('asked') with a ('whether'), and here the verb is oedd, the past form 'was'. Both Ydy …? and Oes …? questions become a oedd: "Oes unrhyw un wedi gweld Rhita?" ('Has anyone seen Rhita?') → Gofynnodd Arthur a oedd unrhyw un wedi gweld Rhita Gawr ('Arthur asked whether anyone had seen Rhita Gawr'); "Ydy'r cawr yn gweld yn dda?" ('Does the giant see well?') → Gofynnodd hi a oedd y cawr yn gweld yn dda ('She asked whether the giant saw well'). Os ('if') is used the same way in speech: Wedyn gofynnodd e os oedd Rhita eisiau heddwch hefyd ('Then he asked if Rhita wanted peace too'). The exercises accept a ydy … too when the question is still true now.

Two other forms appear in Mali's report, for recognition only. The messenger had said "Bydd Rhita'n dod!" ('Rhita will come!'), and Mali reports this as dwedodd y negesydd y byddai Rhita'n dod gyda byddin ('the messenger said that Rhita would come with an army'). Byddai means 'would', and a reported future uses y + byddai instead of fod. Finally, Mali says mae e'n dweud taw ei farf e yw'r farf orau yng Nghymru ('he says that his beard is the best beard in Wales'). When the reported sentence is an identification of the X yw Y kind, southern Welsh uses taw instead of bod. Both y byddai and taw are for recognition only here.
